claim: Epileptic seizures induce aberrant neurogenesis from resident neural stem cells (NSCs) in the dentate gyrus of the adult mouse hippocampus.
source: Epileptic seizures induce aberrant neurogenesis from resident neural stem cells (NSCs) in the dentate gyrus of the adult mouse hippocampus, which has been implicated in depletion of the NSC pool and impairment of hippocampal function.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Jessberger et al., 2007; Jessberger and Parent, 2015; Parent et al., 1997).

claim: Seizure-induced aberrant neurogenesis has been implicated in depletion of the NSC pool and impairment of hippocampal function.
source: Epileptic seizures induce aberrant neurogenesis from resident neural stem cells (NSCs) in the dentate gyrus of the adult mouse hippocampus, which has been implicated in depletion of the NSC pool and impairment of hippocampal function.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research on seizure-induced neurogenesis and its consequences.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (Shh) from mossy cells is a major source of Shh signaling activity after seizures.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Sonic hedgehog (Shh) from mossy cells is a major source of Shh signaling activity after seizures, by which mossy cells contribute to seizure-induced neurogenesis and maintenance of the NSC pool.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing Shh expression in mossy cells and its increase after seizures.

claim: Mossy cells contribute to seizure-induced neurogenesis through Shh signaling.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Sonic hedgehog (Shh) from mossy cells is a major source of Shh signaling activity after seizures, by which mossy cells contribute to seizure-induced neurogenesis and maintenance of the NSC pool.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing that deletion of Shh from mossy cells attenuates seizure-induced neurogenesis.

claim: Deletion of Shh from mossy cells attenuates seizure-induced neurogenesis.
source: Deletion of Shh from mossy cells attenuates seizure-induced neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 3 with quantitative data.

claim: In the absence of Shh from mossy cells, NSC pools are prematurely depleted after seizure-induced proliferation.
source: Moreover, in the absence of Shh from mossy cells, NSCs pool are prematurely depleted after seizure-induced proliferation, and NSCs have impaired self-renewal.
evidence: This is demonstrated through long-term tracing experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: NSCs have impaired self-renewal in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
source: Moreover, in the absence of Shh from mossy cells, NSCs pool are prematurely depleted after seizure-induced proliferation, and NSCs have impaired self-renewal.
evidence: This is shown through BrdU retention experiments measuring NSC persistence after proliferation.

claim: Lack of Shh from mossy cells accelerates age-related decline of the NSC pool.
source: Likewise, lack of Shh from mossy cells accelerates age-related decline of the NSC pool with accompanying reduction of self-renewal of NSCs outside the context of pathology such as seizures.
evidence: This is demonstrated in aged mice (9-11 months) in Figure 6.

claim: Lack of Shh from mossy cells reduces self-renewal of NSCs during aging.
source: Likewise, lack of Shh from mossy cells accelerates age-related decline of the NSC pool with accompanying reduction of self-renewal of NSCs outside the context of pathology such as seizures.
evidence: This is shown through BrdU retention experiments in aged mice.

claim: Shh from mossy cells is critical to maintain NSCs and to prevent exhaustion from excessive consumption in aging and after seizures.
source: Together, our findings indicate that Shh from mossy cells is critical to maintain NSCs and to prevent exhaustion from excessive consumption in aging and after seizures.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined experimental results.

claim: NSCs in the adult DG are maintained in a quiescent state.
source: NSCs in the adult DG are maintained in a quiescent state, thus adult neurogenesis begins by activating NSC proliferation, followed by differentiation and maturation of newborn neurons (Encinas et al., 2011; Lugert et al., 2010; Urbán et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Adult neurogenesis begins by activating NSC proliferation, followed by differentiation and maturation of newborn neurons.
source: NSCs in the adult DG are maintained in a quiescent state, thus adult neurogenesis begins by activating NSC proliferation, followed by differentiation and maturation of newborn neurons (Encinas et al., 2011; Lugert et al., 2010; Urbán et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: NSC proliferation and subsequent differentiation in the adult DG are influenced by neuronal activity and the processing of multiple external stimuli.
source: NSC proliferation and subsequent differentiation in the adult DG are influenced by neuronal activity and the processing of multiple external stimuli and have been shown to be dysregulated after brain insults and in disease states (Kempermann, 2019; Lugert et al., 2010; Moreno-Jiménez et al., 2019; van Praag et al., 1999a; Sierra et al., 2015; Tobin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Epileptic seizures are known to strongly induce adult neurogenesis.
source: Epileptic seizures are known to strongly induce adult neurogenesis (Jessberger et al., 2007; Jessberger and Parent, 2015; Parent et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Increased neurogenesis has been shown to contribute to hippocampus-dependent learning and memory.
source: Normally, increased neurogenesis has been shown to contribute to hippocampus-dependent learning and memory (Deng et al., 2010; Ming and Song, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Seizure-induced newborn neurons have morphological abnormalities.
source: However, seizure-induced newborn neurons have morphological abnormalities, and many ectopically migrate into the hilus of the DG (Parent et al., 1997) contributing to formation of aberrant neuronal circuits in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Many seizure-induced newborn neurons ectopically migrate into the hilus of the DG.
source: However, seizure-induced newborn neurons have morphological abnormalities, and many ectopically migrate into the hilus of the DG (Parent et al., 1997) contributing to formation of aberrant neuronal circuits in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citation and confirmed by data in Figure 1.

claim: Ectopic neurons are implicated in cognitive impairment as well as in the development of repeated spontaneous seizures.
source: These ectopic neurons are implicated in cognitive impairment as well as in the development of repeated spontaneous seizures (Cho et al., 2015; Lybrand et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Once NSC proliferation is activated, NSCs are consumed after a series of cell divisions for neuronal production, resulting in the reduction of neurogenesis and the decline of the NSC pool with age.
source: Furthermore, previous studies showed that once NSC proliferation is activated, NSCs are consumed after a series of cell divisions for neuronal production, resulting in the reduction of neurogenesis and the decline of the NSC pool with age (Encinas et al., 2011; Harris et al., 2021; Lugert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Excessive neuronal production induced by neuronal hyperactivity has been linked to accelerated consumption of NSCs and leads to depletion of the NSC pool.
source: Excessive neuronal production induced by neuronal hyperactivity has been linked to accelerated consumption of NSCs and leads to depletion of the NSC pool (Fu et al., 2019; Sierra et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mossy cells are excitatory neurons in the dentate hilus that provide glutamatergic inputs to newborn granule neurons and GABAergic interneurons in the DG.
source: Mossy cells are excitatory neurons in the dentate hilus that provide glutamatergic inputs to newborn granule neurons and GABAergic interneurons in the DG (Chancey et al., 2014; Scharfman, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mossy cells are among the most sensitive neurons to afferent excitation in the hippocampus.
source: Mossy cells are among the most sensitive neurons to afferent excitation in the hippocampus and are vulnerable to continuous seizures (Scharfman, 1991; Scharfman, 2016; Sloviter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mossy cells are vulnerable to continuous seizures.
source: Mossy cells are among the most sensitive neurons to afferent excitation in the hippocampus and are vulnerable to continuous seizures (Scharfman, 1991; Scharfman, 2016; Sloviter et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Only highly activated mossy cells increase NSC proliferation.
source: Mossy cell activity modulates NSC proliferation depending on the intensity of activation: only highly activated mossy cells increase NSC proliferation (Yeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Shh is expressed by mossy cells.
source: We previously found that Sonic hedgehog (Shh), a morphogen inducing cell proliferation, is expressed by mossy cells (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and confirmed by data in Figure 2.

claim: Increased Shh signaling and Shh expression were observed in the hippocampus of temporal lobe epilepsy patients and epileptic rodent models.
source: Dysregulation of Shh signaling activity has been reported in epileptic seizures where increased Shh signaling and Shh expression were observed in the hippocampus of temporal lobe epilepsy patients and epileptic rodent models (Fang et al., 2011; Pitter et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Increased Shh signaling in NSCs drives NSC proliferation and neurogenesis.
source: Manipulation of Shh receptors in NSCs has shown that increased Shh signaling in NSCs drives NSC proliferation and neurogenesis (Antonelli et al., 2018; Choe and Pleasure, 2013; Daynac et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Gli1-nLacZ+ Shh-responding cells in the SGZ are significantly increased 3 days post-seizure induction.
source: We induced seizures with consecutive intraperitoneal injection of low-dose kainic acid (KA) in Gli1nLacZ/+ mice and found that Gli1-nLacZ+ Shh-responding cells in the SGZ are significantly increased 3 days post-seizure induction (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding shown in Figure 1A and 1B with quantitative data.

claim: Shh signaling activity is increased in NSCs after KA-induced seizures.
source: These data show that Shh signaling activity is increased in NSCs after KA-induced seizures.
evidence: This is concluded from the Gli1-nLacZ data showing increased Shh-responding cells.

claim: About 90% of tdTomato-labeled cells in the SGZ were Sox2+ S100B− cells.
source: One day after a 3-day tamoxifen treatment, we observed that about 90% of tdTomato-labeled cells in the SGZ were Sox2+ S100B− cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), comprising Sox2+ GFAP+ radial glial cell population.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with quantitative data.

claim: NSCs are Shh responsive and Gli1 expression in the SGZ is essentially restricted to NSCs.
source: This confirms that NSCs are Shh responsive and that Gli1 expression in the SGZ is essentially restricted to NSCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the Gli1CreER lineage tracing data.

claim: Gli1-nLacZ+ Shh-responding cells in the SGZ of Shh+/−; Gli1nLacZ/+ mice were significantly reduced.
source: We found that Gli1-nLacZ+ Shh-responding cells in the SGZ of Shh+/−; Gli1nLacZ/+ mice were significantly reduced (Figure 1C, D), indicating that the level of Shh signaling in NSCs is decreased in these mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and 1D with quantitative data.

claim: Gli1-nLacZ+ cells failed to increase after seizure induction in Shh+/− mice.
source: We also observed that Gli1-nLacZ+ cells failed to increase after seizure induction in these mice, indicating that Shh signaling activity is not upregulated with seizure activity in Shh+/− mice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with quantitative data.

claim: The number of BrdU+ DCX+ newborn neurons dramatically increased after seizure induction in WT mice.
source: In WT mice, the number of BrdU+ DCX+ newborn neurons dramatically increased after seizure induction. However, this was significantly reduced in Shh+/− mice by comparison (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F-H with quantitative data.

claim: The increase in BrdU+ DCX+ newborn neurons after seizure induction was significantly reduced in Shh+/− mice compared to WT mice.
source: In WT mice, the number of BrdU+ DCX+ newborn neurons dramatically increased after seizure induction. However, this was significantly reduced in Shh+/− mice by comparison (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F-H with quantitative data.

claim: Shh+/− mice have a reduction in ectopic hilar dentate neurons.
source: Shh+/− mice have a reduction in ectopic hilar dentate neurons (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I with quantitative data.

claim: Shh contributes to seizure-induced aberrant neurogenesis.
source: These results demonstrate that Shh contributes to seizure-induced aberrant neurogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing reduced neurogenesis in Shh+/− mice after seizures.

claim: The majority of tdTomato+ cells in the dentate hilus were GluR2/3+ mossy cells.
source: Co-immunostaining with the cell-type markers showed that the majority of tdTomato+ cells were GluR2/3+ mossy cells but with a much smaller number of Parvalbumin+ interneurons expressing tdTomato (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D with quantitative data.

claim: A much smaller number of Parvalbumin+ interneurons express tdTomato in ShhCre/+;RosaAI14 mice.
source: Co-immunostaining with the cell-type markers showed that the majority of tdTomato+ cells were GluR2/3+ mossy cells but with a much smaller number of Parvalbumin+ interneurons expressing tdTomato (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and 2D with quantitative data.

claim: The cell types reflected in the population of tdTomato+ cells did not change with seizure induction.
source: Furthermore, the cell types reflected in the population of tdTomato+ cells did not change with seizure induction, thus indicating that in the hilus, seizures did not lead to ectopic expression of Shh in cells that normally do not express the ligand (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with quantitative data.

claim: tdTomato+ cells were dominantly observed in the dorsal GluR2/3+ mossy cells but not in the ventral hippocampus.
source: Interestingly, we found that tdTomato+ cells were dominantly observed in the dorsal GluR2/3+ mossy cells but not in the ventral hippocampus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dorsal mossy cells are the major source of Shh in DG in both the naive and post-seizure hippocampus.
source: These data suggest that dorsal mossy cells are the major source of Shh in DG in both the naive and post-seizure hippocampus.
evidence: This is concluded from the lineage tracing data showing Shh expression predominantly in dorsal mossy cells.

claim: Shh mRNA is enriched in the dentate hilus.
source: Consistent with the results from ShhCre/+;RosaAI14 mice, we observed that Shh mRNA is enriched in the dentate hilus (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E using RNAscope in situ hybridization.

claim: Shh expression was dramatically increased throughout the dentate hilus from anterior to posterior of dorsal DG at 24 hr after seizure induction.
source: Furthermore, Shh expression was dramatically increased throughout the dentate hilus from anterior to posterior of dorsal DG at 24 hr after seizure induction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E using RNAscope in situ hybridization.

claim: Shh mRNA in GluR2/3+ mossy cells was significantly increased after seizure induction.
source: Combining RNAscope with immunofluorescence, we analyzed the number of Shh mRNA puncta in the GluR2/3+ mossy cells and found significantly increased Shh in mossy cells after seizure induction (Figure 2F, G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F and 2G with quantitative data.

claim: Mossy cells are the local source of Shh in the DG.
source: Taken together, these data support the conclusion that mossy cells are the local source of Shh in the DG and that Shh mRNA expression is increased upon seizure activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined lineage tracing and RNAscope data.

claim: Shh mRNA expression is increased upon seizure activity.
source: Taken together, these data support the conclusion that mossy cells are the local source of Shh in the DG and that Shh mRNA expression is increased upon seizure activity.
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: The number of Gli1-nLacZ+ cells was significantly decreased in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice.
source: We found that the number of Gli1-nLacZ+ cells was significantly decreased in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice (Crlr-Cre;Shh+/+ mice and Shh+/+, Shhfl/+ and Shhfl/fl without the Cre transgene were used as controls) (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B with quantitative data.

claim: The increase in Gli1-nLacZ+ cells after seizure induction was not observed in Shh-cKO;Gli1nLacZ/+ mice.
source: Three days after seizure induction, Gli1-nLacZ+ cells were significantly increased in control mice. However, this increase was not observed in Shh-cKO;Gli1nLacZ/+ mice, in which Gli1-nLacZ+ cells were rarely detected in the SGZ.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and 3B with quantitative data.

claim: There were comparable number of Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice.
source: We found that there were comparable number of Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that reduction of Gli1-nLacZ+ cells is not due to general loss of NSCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with quantitative data.

claim: Shh from mossy cells is responsible for Shh signaling in the DG.
source: These data suggest that Shh from mossy cells is responsible for Shh signaling in the DG, and that Shh signaling fails to be upregulated by seizures in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the Gli1-nLacZ data in Shh-cKO mice.

claim: Shh signaling fails to be upregulated by seizures in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
source: These data suggest that Shh from mossy cells is responsible for Shh signaling in the DG, and that Shh signaling fails to be upregulated by seizures in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
evidence: This is shown by the lack of increase in Gli1-nLacZ+ cells after seizures in Shh-cKO mice.

claim: The number of DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons was comparable between control and Shh-cKO mice in the KA treatment-naive condition.
source: We found that the number of DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons was comparable between control and Shh-cKO mice in the KA treatment-naive condition, suggesting that deletion of Shh from mossy cells does not significantly affect baseline neurogenesis in this timeframe.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and 3E with quantitative data.

claim: Deletion of Shh from mossy cells does not significantly affect baseline neurogenesis in the timeframe studied.
source: We found that the number of DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons was comparable between control and Shh-cKO mice in the KA treatment-naive condition, suggesting that deletion of Shh from mossy cells does not significantly affect baseline neurogenesis in this timeframe.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparable neurogenesis in naive conditions.

claim: The number of BrdU+ DCX+ newborn neurons was significantly reduced in Shh-cKO mice compared to control mice after seizure induction.
source: However, we found that the number of BrdU+ DCX+ newborn neurons was significantly reduced in Shh-cKO mice compared to control mice after seizure induction (Figure 3D, E), indicating that deletion of Shh in mossy cells attenuates seizure-induced neurogenesis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and 3E with quantitative data.

claim: Mossy cells function as a critical source of Shh for Shh signaling activity of NSCs.
source: Together, these data indicate that mossy cells function as a critical source of Shh for Shh signaling activity of NSCs, and that Shh derived from mossy cells contributes to seizure-induced neurogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data showing reduced Shh signaling and neurogenesis in Shh-cKO mice.

claim: Shh derived from mossy cells contributes to seizure-induced neurogenesis.
source: Together, these data indicate that mossy cells function as a critical source of Shh for Shh signaling activity of NSCs, and that Shh derived from mossy cells contributes to seizure-induced neurogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduced neurogenesis in Shh-cKO mice after seizures.

claim: Over 90% of mCherry+ expressing cells are GluR2/3+ mossy cells in Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice.
source: As previously reported, we found that over 90% of mCherry+ expressing cells are GluR2/3+ mossy cells (Jinde et al., 2012), and that these made up 65% of the GluR2/3+ mossy cells in the dentate hilus (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and 4D with quantitative data.

claim: mCherry+ cells made up 65% of the GluR2/3+ mossy cells in the dentate hilus in Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice.
source: As previously reported, we found that over 90% of mCherry+ expressing cells are GluR2/3+ mossy cells (Jinde et al., 2012), and that these made up 65% of the GluR2/3+ mossy cells in the dentate hilus (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and 4D with quantitative data.

claim: Expression of c-fos was significantly increased in the hilus of Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice 1.5 hr after CLZ injection.
source: 1.5 hr after CLZ injection, we observed that expression of c-fos, a marker of neuronal activation, was significantly increased in the hilus of Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice (Figure 4E, F); we also confirmed that over 70% of GluR2/3+ mCherry+ mossy cells were activated (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and 4F with quantitative data.

claim: Over 70% of GluR2/3+ mCherry+ mossy cells were activated after CLZ injection in Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice.
source: 1.5 hr after CLZ injection, we observed that expression of c-fos, a marker of neuronal activation, was significantly increased in the hilus of Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice (Figure 4E, F); we also confirmed that over 70% of GluR2/3+ mCherry+ mossy cells were activated (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G with quantitative data.

claim: The number of DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons was significantly increased in Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice after CLZ treatment.
source: We found that the number of DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons was significantly increased in Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice (Figure 4I, J), suggesting that increased neuronal activity of mossy cells drove neurogenesis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I and 4J with quantitative data.

claim: Increased neuronal activity of mossy cells drove neurogenesis.
source: We found that the number of DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons was significantly increased in Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq mice (Figure 4I, J), suggesting that increased neuronal activity of mossy cells drove neurogenesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the increased neurogenesis after chemogenetic activation of mossy cells.

claim: Gli1-nLacZ+ cells were significantly increased in the SGZ of Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq;Gli1nLacZ/+ mice after CLZ administration.
source: After 6 days of CLZ administration (Figure 4K), we found that Gli1-nLacZ+ were significantly increased in the SGZ of Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq;Gli1nLacZ/+ mice, compared with RosaDIO-hM3Dq;Gli1nLacZ/+ control mice (Figure 4L, M), suggesting that Shh signaling activity is upregulated in NSCs by mossy cell neuronal activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4L and 4M with quantitative data.

claim: Shh signaling activity is upregulated in NSCs by mossy cell neuronal activity.
source: After 6 days of CLZ administration (Figure 4K), we found that Gli1-nLacZ+ were significantly increased in the SGZ of Crlr-Cre;hM3Dq;Gli1nLacZ/+ mice, compared with RosaDIO-hM3Dq;Gli1nLacZ/+ control mice (Figure 4L, M), suggesting that Shh signaling activity is upregulated in NSCs by mossy cell neuronal activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the increased Gli1-nLacZ+ cells after mossy cell activation.

claim: There was no induction of neurogenesis by mossy cell neuronal activity in Crlr-Cre;Shhfl/fl;hM3Dq mice after CLZ administration.
source: After CLZ administration, we found no induction of neurogenesis by mossy cell neuronal activity in Crlr-Cre;Shhfl/fl;hM3Dq mice (Figure 4N, O), indicating that induction of neurogenesis by mossy cell neuronal activity is compromised in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4N and 4O with quantitative data.

claim: Induction of neurogenesis by mossy cell neuronal activity is compromised in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
source: After CLZ administration, we found no induction of neurogenesis by mossy cell neuronal activity in Crlr-Cre;Shhfl/fl;hM3Dq mice (Figure 4N, O), indicating that induction of neurogenesis by mossy cell neuronal activity is compromised in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of neurogenesis induction in Shh-deleted mossy cells.

claim: Shh from mossy cells contributes to neuronal activity-induced neurogenesis by mossy cells.
source: Together, these data indicate that Shh from mossy cells contributes to neuronal activity-induced neurogenesis by mossy cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined DREADD experiments.

claim: The number of newborn neurons was significantly increased on the contralateral DG of AAV::hM3Dq-mCherry-injected mice after CLZ treatment.
source: We found that the number of newborn neurons was significantly increased on the contralateral DG of AAV::hM3Dq-mCherry-injected mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I, J), indicating that mossy cell neuronal activity contributes to increasing neurogenesis in the contralateral DG.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I and J with quantitative data.

claim: Mossy cell neuronal activity contributes to increasing neurogenesis in the contralateral DG.
source: We found that the number of newborn neurons was significantly increased on the contralateral DG of AAV::hM3Dq-mCherry-injected mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I, J), indicating that mossy cell neuronal activity contributes to increasing neurogenesis in the contralateral DG.
evidence: This is concluded from the increased neurogenesis in the contralateral DG after unilateral mossy cell activation.

claim: Seizure-induced neurogenesis was attenuated in the contralateral DG of mice injected with AAV::Cre-tdTomato.
source: We then tested whether Shh deletion affects contralateral neurogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E) and found that seizure-induced neurogenesis was attenuated in the contralateral DG of mice injected with AAV::Cre-tdTomato, in which DCX+ BrdU+ newborn neurons induced by seizure activity were significantly reduced compared with mice injected with AAV::mCherry control virus (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F, G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F and G with quantitative data.

claim: Mossy cells control contralateral neurogenesis by regulating Shh expression after seizures.
source: This suggests that mossy cells control contralateral neurogenesis by regulating Shh expression after seizures.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduced contralateral neurogenesis after unilateral Shh deletion.

claim: Increased Shh following seizures may be transported and contribute to neurogenesis in the contralateral DG.
source: Together with our findings that Shh expression was increased by seizure (Figure 2F, G), these data demonstrate that increased Shh following seizures may be transported and contribute to neurogenesis in the contralateral DG.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on Shh transport and contralateral effects.

claim: Mossy cells release Shh with increased neuronal activity and induce neurogenesis driven by seizures.
source: Taken together, these data support our hypothesis that mossy cells release Shh with increased neuronal activity and induce neurogenesis driven by seizures (Figure 4P).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the combined experimental results, illustrated in Figure 4P.

claim: Seizure induction increases the number of BrdU+ Sox2+ proliferating NSCs at day 0 in both control and Shh-cKO mice compared with the no seizure condition.
source: We found that seizure induction increases the number of BrdU+ Sox2+ proliferating NSCs at day 0 (last day of BrdU labeling) in both control and Shh-cKO mice compared with the no seizure condition, although it was significantly attenuated in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and 5D with quantitative data.

claim: The increase in BrdU+ Sox2+ proliferating NSCs after seizure was significantly attenuated in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice.
source: We found that seizure induction increases the number of BrdU+ Sox2+ proliferating NSCs at day 0 (last day of BrdU labeling) in both control and Shh-cKO mice compared with the no seizure condition, although it was significantly attenuated in Shh-cKO mice compared with control mice (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and 5D with quantitative data.

claim: The number of BrdU-retaining Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs was increased in seizure-induced mice compared with no seizure-induced mice at 4 weeks after BrdU labeling.
source: Four weeks after BrdU labeling, we found that the number of BrdU-retaining Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs was increased in seizure-induced mice compared with no seizure-induced mice, as expected from the increased proliferation after seizure (Figure 5C, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and 5E with quantitative data.

claim: The number of BrdU-retaining Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs in Shh-cKO mice was significantly reduced compared with seizure-induced control mice at 4 weeks.
source: However, the number of BrdU-retaining Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs in Shh-cKO mice was significantly reduced compared with seizure-induced control mice (Figure 5C, E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and 5E with quantitative data.

claim: The fraction of NSCs that retain stem cell identity after proliferation was comparable in control mice with and without seizure induction.
source: We found that the fraction of NSCs that retain stem cell identity after proliferation was comparable in control mice with and without seizure induction. This indicates that even though seizures induce NSCs to proliferate, they return to the stem cell state in the same ratio (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F with quantitative data.

claim: The fraction of NSCs that returned to the stem cell state in Shh-cKO mice was significantly reduced after seizure-induced proliferation.
source: In contrast, we found that the fraction of NSCs that returned to the stem cell state in Shh-cKO mice was significantly reduced after seizure-induced proliferation (Figure 5F), suggesting that NSCs are less likely to return to their stem cell state after seizure-induced proliferation in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F with quantitative data.

claim: NSCs are less likely to return to their stem cell state after seizure-induced proliferation in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
source: In contrast, we found that the fraction of NSCs that returned to the stem cell state in Shh-cKO mice was significantly reduced after seizure-induced proliferation (Figure 5F), suggesting that NSCs are less likely to return to their stem cell state after seizure-induced proliferation in the absence of Shh from mossy cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduced NSC persistence in Shh-cKO mice.

claim: The number of Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs in the SGZ of control mice is comparable with and without seizures at 5 weeks after seizure induction.
source: We found that the number of Sox2+ GFAP+ radial NSCs in the SGZ of control mice is comparable with and without seizures, suggesting that the NSC pool size is maintained at least 5 weeks after seizure induction in control mice (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G and 5H with quantitative data.
